questions.title: Locating a period-3 element
questions.stem: Element X belongs to period 3. Its first four successive ionization energies are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11578 kJ mol⁻¹. In a separate experiment an isolated X atom absorbs a photon just sufficient for its first ionization. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c=3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹ and NA=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X and use the pattern, rather than a lookup, to explain your assignment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give the full configuration of X, that of X³⁺, and the type of orbital from which the fourth electron is removed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the longest wavelength that can ionize the neutral atom in its ground state.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Compare ionizing a ground-state atom with producing an emission line between two bound states. Relate each to the convergence limit.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A 220 nm photon strikes ground-state X. Determine whether single-photon ionization is possible and explain why the atom need not absorb this photon even if its energy is below the threshold.

steps.text: The largest jump is between IE₃ and IE₄.
Three outer electrons can be removed before a core electron is reached.
Period 3 and three outer electrons identify aluminium.
X: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹.
X³⁺: 1s²2s²2p⁶.
The fourth electron is removed from a 2p orbital.
Energy per atom=578000/(6.02×10²³)=9.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
λ=hc/E.
Ionization removes the electron to the continuum; a bound-state transition leaves it on the atom.
Emission releases a photon equal in energy to the difference between the two bound levels.
Bound levels become closer at high energy; convergence to the continuum from the ground level corresponds to the first ionization energy.
220 nm is longer than 207 nm, so its energy is below threshold.
It cannot ionize ground-state X by single-photon absorption.
Below threshold a photon must match an allowed bound-state energy gap to be absorbed.

questions.answerSummary: Below threshold a photon must match an allowed bound-state energy gap to be absorbed.

questions.title: Two fluorides in a sealed vessel
questions.stem: Molecular XeF₄ and SF₄ are compared in the gas phase. Xenon has eight valence electrons; sulfur has six. Treat all Xe–F and S–F bonds as single in the Lewis models.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the number of electron domains, lone pairs and molecular geometry around Xe in XeF₄.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce the geometry of SF₄ and explain the preferred position of its lone pair.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the expected permanent dipole moments and distinguish bond from molecular polarity.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: For the Lewis model of XeF₄, show the formal charge on Xe and one F. State why zero formal charge does not imply a nonpolar bond.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Replace one F of square planar XeF₄ by Cl without changing the arrangement. Predict whether the four ligand positions were equivalent before replacement, whether a dipole is expected after replacement, and why.

steps.text: Four bonding pairs plus two lone pairs give six domains.
The two lone pairs occupy opposite positions in an octahedral domain arrangement.
The atoms form a square planar molecule.
Four bonds and one lone pair give five domains (trigonal bipyramidal).
An equatorial lone pair has fewer 90° interactions than an axial lone pair.
The resulting molecular geometry is seesaw.
The electronegativity differences make the individual bonds polar.
Equal Xe–F bond dipoles cancel in square planar XeF₄.
The seesaw arrangement in SF₄ does not cancel the bond dipoles; it is polar.
Formal charge divides bonding electrons equally by convention; electron density is not shared equally in a polar bond.
All four positions in XeF₄ are symmetry-equivalent.
Replacement preserves cancellation of one opposing F–Xe–F pair.
Xe–Cl and the opposing Xe–F do not generally have equal bond dipoles, giving a net dipole.

questions.answerSummary: Xe–Cl and the opposing Xe–F do not generally have equal bond dipoles, giving a net dipole.

questions.title: Dissociation of nitrogen dioxide
questions.stem: For 2NO₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)+O₂(g), use ΔH°=+114.2 kJ and ΔS°=+146.4 J K⁻¹ per reaction as written. Assume constant values over the range considered. For an ideal gas the activity is its partial pressure divided by 1.00 bar. Use ΔG=ΔG°+RT ln Q and R=8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the sign of ΔS° and determine the standard-state crossover temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate ΔG° and K at 700 K.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At equilibrium p(NO)/p(NO₂)=0.500. Deduce the oxygen partial pressure, showing the expression for K.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Oxygen is selectively removed, briefly leaving p(O₂)=0.100 bar and the same NO:NO₂ pressure ratio. Calculate ΔG at 700 K and predict the net reaction direction.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Determine the heat released by forming 0.750 mol NO₂ via the reverse reaction. Explain why a catalyst does not change the heat per mole for fixed reactant and product states.

steps.text: The number of gas particles increases from two to three, increasing dispersal.
At crossover ΔG°=0 and T=ΔH°/ΔS°.
K=[a(NO)/a(NO₂)]² a(O₂).
p(O₂)≈0.533 bar.
Net forward reaction replaces some removed oxygen.
Reverse ΔH°=−114.2 kJ per 2 mol NO₂.
A catalyst changes activation energies but not the enthalpy difference between states.

questions.answerSummary: A catalyst changes activation energies but not the enthalpy difference between states.

questions.title: A buffer with a limited reserve
questions.stem: At 298 K a solution is made from 40.00 cm³ of 0.2000 mol dm⁻³ methanoic acid and 30.00 cm³ of 0.2000 mol dm⁻³ sodium methanoate. Ka=1.80×10⁻⁴ and Kw=1.00×10⁻¹⁴. Assume additive volumes and ideal concentrations.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial pH using the buffer approximation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: 10.00 cm³ of 0.1000 mol dm⁻³ HCl is added. Show the chemical change and calculate the new pH.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the further volume of 0.1000 mol dm⁻³ HCl needed to consume the remaining analytical methanoate. Explain why the original buffer formula then fails.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: At this point estimate the pH from the weak acid equilibrium, using a small-dissociation approximation and checking it afterwards.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Evaluate two claims: dilution by a factor of two doubles buffer capacity expressed per litre, and dilution substantially changes the original buffer pH. Distinguish total amount from concentration.

steps.text: pKa=3.745; pH=pKa+log(n(A⁻)/n(HA)).
A⁻+H⁺→HA consumes 0.001000 mol A⁻.
New amounts: 0.005000 mol A⁻ and 0.009000 mol HA.
A further 0.005000 mol HCl is required.
The added conjugate base has been consumed; its amount cannot be treated as a large independently fixed buffer component.
There is 0.01400 mol acid in 0.1300 dm³, C=0.1077 mol dm⁻³.
Ka=x²/(C−x); x≈0.00431 mol dm⁻³ (or approximately 0.00440 since dissociation is about 4%).
pH≈2.37; accept 2.36 with the stated approximation.
Dilution halves the amounts of acid and base per litre, so capacity per litre decreases.
For the whole sample the analytical moles available to consume added acid or base remain the same.
The ratio of conjugate-base to acid concentrations remains approximately constant, so ideal buffer pH changes little.

questions.answerSummary: The ratio of conjugate-base to acid concentrations remains approximately constant, so ideal buffer pH changes little.

questions.title: Testing an elementary-step model
questions.stem: A gas reaction obeys 2NO+O₂→2NO₂. A proposed mechanism is 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast pre-equilibrium), then N₂O₂+O₂→2NO₂ (slow). At fixed initial concentrations the initial rate at 320 K is 2.50 times that at 300 K. Use R=8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the intermediate and show that summing the forward steps gives the observed overall equation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive the predicted rate law in terms of reactants only.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the rate change if [NO] is halved and [O₂] tripled at fixed temperature; state overall order and units for the observed k when concentration is in mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Estimate the apparent activation energy from the temperature pair.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Assess whether agreement with this rate law proves the mechanism. Suggest additional evidence and explain why the apparent activation energy need not equal the slow step’s barrier.

steps.text: N₂O₂ is formed then consumed and is absent from the net equation.
Add 2NO→N₂O₂ and N₂O₂+O₂→2NO₂.
Cancel N₂O₂ to recover 2NO+O₂→2NO₂.
Slow elementary step: rate=k₂[N₂O₂][O₂].
Fast pre-equilibrium: [N₂O₂]=K₁[NO]².
Therefore rate=k₂K₁[NO]²[O₂].
Rate factor=(½)²×3=0.75.
Overall order is three.
k has units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
Ea=36.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
Different mechanisms can yield the same empirical law.
Detection of transient N₂O₂, for example spectroscopically, would test the intermediate prediction.
Observed k=k₂K₁, so temperature dependence contains both slow-step and pre-equilibrium contributions.

questions.answerSummary: Observed k=k₂K₁, so temperature dependence contains both slow-step and pre-equilibrium contributions.

questions.title: An ester and its hydrolysis products
questions.stem: A saturated acyclic ester has formula C₅H₁₀O₂. Its ¹H NMR spectrum has a 6H doublet, a 1H septet near 5.0 ppm and a 3H singlet near 2.0 ppm. A sample of 2.040 g reacts completely with aqueous NaOH; M(ester)=102.0 g mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the splitting and integration of the doublet and septet to identify a fragment and its location relative to oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce the complete ester structure and explain the singlet, giving the systematic name.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the equation for alkaline hydrolysis and calculate the minimum volume of 0.2500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH needed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: An excess of aqueous acid is then added to the cooled mixture. Identify the organic acid formed, write the responsible ionic equation and identify a diagnostic IR change for the isolated dry acid compared with the original ester.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Predict the main product on controlled oxidation of the alcohol hydrolysis product and identify two expected changes in its ¹H NMR spectrum.

steps.text: A 6H doublet indicates two equivalent methyl groups adjacent to one proton.
A 1H septet indicates a CH coupled to six equivalent methyl protons.
The downfield CH is bonded to ester oxygen: –OCH(CH₃)₂.
Structure CH₃C(=O)OCH(CH₃)₂.
The acetyl methyl has no adjacent proton across the carbonyl carbon, so is a singlet.
Propan-2-yl ethanoate (isopropyl acetate accepted).
CH₃COOCH(CH₃)₂+NaOH→CH₃COONa+(CH₃)₂CHOH.
n(ester)=2.040/102.0=0.02000 mol; one equivalent hydroxide is needed.
Ethanoic acid forms.
CH₃COO⁻+H⁺→CH₃COOH.
The acid has a very broad O–H absorption around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, absent in the ester.
Propan-2-ol gives propanone.
The proton on the carbon bearing OH is absent in propanone.
The methyl doublet becomes one 6H singlet since there is no neighbouring CH proton.

questions.answerSummary: The methyl doublet becomes one 6H singlet since there is no neighbouring CH proton.
